title: After Finishing My Dispatched Study Abroad at the University of Western Australia
paragraphs: I did clerkships for one month in Perth, the home base of the University of Western Australia, and for one month in Albany, the southernmost town in the state of Western Australia.

In Perth, at Sir Charles Gardner Hospital, I did two weeks each of clerkship in rheumatology and clinical immunology. Since they are departments with few procedures and few inpatients, the main content of the clerkship was outpatient observation and physical examination. Because Nagoya University does not have either as an organized clinical department, I was able to learn, together with the patients' own voices and physical findings, about diseases that I had until then seen only in textbooks. During rounds I also had several opportunities to write in the chart. Although it is a large hospital of more than 600 beds, paper charts were used in almost all departments except the ICU, and I often struggled to decipher handwriting, but I was able to enjoy the difference in systems. In clinical immunology I was also able to learn about immune-related diseases from various angles, by attending a study session for residents, assisting with allergy antigen identification tests, and looking at immunofluorescence-stained kidney and skin specimens. Because it is a hospital where patients gather from all over Western Australia, patients whose symptoms were stable received remote consultations by video call from a town 400 km away, and being able to see that also left an impression.

In Albany, together with students learning in rural medicine, I did one week each at two general practice clinics and two weeks of clerkship at a regional core hospital. This town is the southernmost town in Western Australia, facing the Southern Ocean, with a population of about 37,000. It was a very lovely town where you reach an emerald-blue sea and white sand beach within five minutes by car. Because I had told them that I wanted to know about cooperation between general practice and specialists, they arranged a program that fulfilled this wish even though it was originally outside the period for accepting exchange students. In this town, ten medical students in total from the University of Western Australia and the University of Notre Dame do a clerkship for one year. Both the doctors and the students were full of charm, and I spent unforgettable days.

At the regional core hospital, I was looked after by the general medicine team for two weeks. The educational program for students was very full, and twice a week there was a teaching round, an opportunity for students and doctors, one-to-one, to practice history taking, physical examination, interpretation of test results and case presentations. I took part in this several times too, and although I was overwhelmed by the excellent performance of the other students, I was able to practice history taking and physical examination under the doctor's supervision. Besides this, so that the local students could have as good a clerkship as possible, they looked every day for patients with characteristic findings and had them practice history taking, physical examination and presentations. I also observed the outpatient clinic of a doctor specializing in palliative care and was present at the moment of deciding whether to continue anticancer drug treatment, which also remains strongly in my memory.

In Albany, I met a wonderful doctor who became my role model, and he said to me the very happy words, "You can come back anytime. I'll hire you at my hospital." The doctors, students and patients all understood that English is a second language, and what stayed in my heart was that even when I was at a loss for words, no one made a sour face and they waited, saying warmly, "Take your time to think. I know you can speak."

In addition to the university being one with a short history of exchange partnership, I was the only student sent this year, so I often felt anxious before departure, but supported by the gentle character of the Australian people and the beautiful great nature, I was able to finish my study abroad safely. I sincerely think that taking on this exchange program was the most valuable decision of my six years of university life.
I am deeply grateful to the doctors of both universities, in Western Australia and in Nagoya, who made every effort to make it a fulfilling study abroad.
